fields.headline:
Unit 3
Forces and Motion
fields.subhead: Newton's laws, free body diagrams, inclines, F = ma, friction, and pulleys.

imageSubjects.hero: a loaded freight cart on a ramp with a rope and pulley, dramatic side light

fields.headline:
3.1
Newton's Laws
fields.subhead: Measure forces in newtons, separate mass from weight, and use Newton's three laws.

imageSubjects.section: a cast-iron weight hanging from a spring scale against a dark wall

fields.headline: What Is a Force?
fields.subhead: Every force you draw this unit has two parts: a size and a direction.
fields.a1_b: A force is a push or a pull on an object.
fields.a2_b: 1 N is about the weight of a small apple.
fields.a3_b: Force is a vector: a size plus a direction.

fields.headline: Mass vs. Weight
fields.subhead: They are not the same quantity, and they do not use the same unit.
fields.c1_b:
Amount of matter, in kg.
The same everywhere.
fields.c2_b:
Pull of gravity, in N.
W = mg, g = 9.8 m/s²
Changes with location.
fields.mustwrite: Weight is a force: W = mg, in newtons. Mass is in kilograms.

fields.headline: Weight on Earth and on the Moon
fields.subhead: On the Moon, g = 1.6 m/s².
fields.problem: A 60 kg student stands on Earth, then on the Moon. Find the weight in each place.
fields.q1_b:
m = 60 kg
g Earth = 9.8 m/s²
g Moon = 1.6 m/s²
fields.q2_b: W = mg
fields.answer: Earth: 588 N down  ·  Moon: 96 N down

fields.headline: Newton's First Law
fields.subhead: An object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts on it. Fnet = 0 is equilibrium: at rest or at constant velocity.
fields.keyq: A puck slides at constant speed. Net force? Zero.

fields.headline: Newton's Second Law
fields.subhead: A net force makes an object accelerate. We put numbers on it in 3.4.
fields.c1_b:
Same mass, bigger push.
More acceleration.
fields.c2_b:
Same push, bigger mass.
Less acceleration.
fields.mustwrite: A net force causes acceleration. No net force, no acceleration.

fields.headline: Newton's Third Law
fields.subhead: For every force, the other object pushes back equally, in the opposite direction.
fields.c1_b:
Book pushes on table.
Table pushes on book.
Two different objects.
fields.c2_b:
W and N both act
on the book.
Same object: not a pair.
fields.mustwrite: Action-reaction pairs act on different objects, so they never cancel.

fields.headline:
3.2
Free Body Diagrams
fields.subhead: Draw free body diagrams, find the net force, and break angled forces into components.

imageSubjects.section: a tug-of-war rope pulled taut across a gym floor

fields.headline: Drawing a Free Body Diagram
fields.subhead: One arrow per force, never one for motion. Friction waits until 3.6.
fields.a1_b: A box or dot, one labeled arrow per force, to scale.
fields.a2_b: Weight W, normal N, applied F_app, tension T.
fields.a3_b: A rope only pulls, along the rope, away from the object.

fields.headline: Draw the FBDs
fields.subhead: Both objects are at rest, so the forces on each one balance.
fields.problem: Draw and label FBDs: a 2.0 kg book on a table, and a 1.5 kg lamp hanging from a cord.
fields.q1_b:
Book: m = 2.0 kg
Lamp: m = 1.5 kg
Both at rest
fields.q2_b:
W = mg
At rest: Fnet = 0
fields.answer: Book: N = W = 19.6 N  ·  Lamp: T = W = 14.7 N

fields.headline: Net Force in One Dimension
fields.subhead: Add the forces along each axis, with signs.
fields.c1_b:
Right and up are +.
Left and down are −.
State it every time.
fields.c2_b:
Fnet,x: the horizontals.
Fnet,y: the verticals.
Never mix the two.
fields.mustwrite: Net force is the sum of every force, with signs: Fnet = F1 + F2 + ...

fields.headline: Net Force and Equilibrium
fields.subhead: Use +x right and +y up.
fields.problem: Find the net force on the crate, then the one force that would put it in equilibrium.
fields.q1_b:
50 N right, 20 N left
40 N up, 40 N down
fields.q2_b:
Fnet,x = 50 − 20
Fnet,y = 40 − 40
fields.answer: Fnet = 30 N right  ·  Balancing force: 30 N left

fields.headline: Resultant and Angle
fields.subhead: When Fnet,x and Fnet,y are both nonzero, combine them into one force.
fields.f1_b:
F = √(Fx² + Fy²)
angle = tan inverse (Fy/Fx)
measured from +x
fields.mustwrite: A resultant needs a size and a direction. State both, every time.

fields.headline: Forces at Angles
fields.subhead: Break an angled force into the part along x and the part along y.
fields.a3_b: √(87² + 50²) = 100 N. The parts rebuild the force.

fields.headline: One Angled Force, One Straight
fields.subhead: Seen from above, on frictionless ice. Use +x right.
fields.problem: Two ropes pull a crate: 80 N at 40° above +x, and 30 N toward −x. Find the net force.
fields.q2_b:
Fx = F cos(angle)
Fy = F sin(angle)

fields.headline: Two Angled Forces
fields.subhead: Seen from above. Angles are measured from the x-axis.
fields.problem: Two tugboats pull a barge: 500 N at 30° above +x, 400 N at 45° above −x. Find Fnet.
fields.q2_b:
Sum Fx, sum Fy, then
F = √(Fx² + Fy²)

fields.headline:
3.3
Inclined Plane FBDs
fields.subhead: Tilt the axes and split the weight into parts along and into the slope.

imageSubjects.section: a wooden ramp leaning against a loading dock in low light

fields.headline: Tilt the Axes on a Slope
fields.subhead: The angle between W and the tilted y-axis equals the ramp angle.
fields.a1_b: x along the slope, y perpendicular to the slope.
fields.a2_b: mg sin(angle), pointing down the slope.
fields.a3_b: mg cos(angle), pressing into the surface.

fields.headline: Normal Force Is Not the Weight
fields.subhead: The steeper the ramp, the less the surface pushes back.
fields.c1_b:
N gets close to mg.
Almost nothing pulls
the block along.
fields.c2_b:
N gets close to 0.
The pull along the
slope nears mg.
fields.mustwrite: On an incline, N = mg cos(angle), not mg.

fields.headline: Block on a 30° Ramp
fields.subhead: Frictionless. Tilt your axes before you calculate anything.
fields.problem: A 5.0 kg block sits on a 30° ramp. Draw its FBD. Find both weight components and N.
fields.q2_b:
along: mg sin(angle)
into: mg cos(angle)
fields.answer: Along: 24.5 N  ·  Into: 42.4 N  ·  N = 42.4 N

fields.headline: Net Force Along the Slope
fields.subhead: Frictionless. The push is parallel to the ramp.
fields.problem: A worker pushes a 12 kg crate up a 25° ramp with 30 N. Find the net force along the ramp.
fields.q1_b:
m = 12 kg, angle = 25°
push = 30 N up the ramp
fields.q2_b: Fnet = mg sin(angle) − 30

fields.headline:
3.4
F = ma Calculations
fields.subhead: Use Newton's second law to connect net force, mass, and acceleration.

imageSubjects.section: a lab cart on a track with a hanging mass at the far end

fields.headline: Newton's Second Law: Fnet = ma
fields.subhead: The acceleration is in the direction of the net force.
fields.f1_b:
Fnet = ma
1 N = 1 kg·m/s²
a = Fnet/m
fields.work:
a = 12 N / 4.0 kg
= 3.0 m/s²
to the right
fields.mustwrite: Fnet = ma. Use the net force, never a single force.

fields.headline: Two Opposing Forces
fields.subhead: Use forward as positive.
fields.problem: A 1500 kg car has 4500 N of engine force forward and 1200 N of drag. Find a.
fields.q1_b:
m = 1500 kg
4500 N forward
1200 N backward
fields.q2_b:
Fnet = 4500 − 1200
a = Fnet/m

fields.headline: Reading an F vs. a Graph
fields.subhead: Plot net force against acceleration for one object.
fields.a1_b: Net force on y, acceleration on x.
fields.a3_b: Zero net force gives zero acceleration.

fields.headline: Mass from a Graph
fields.subhead: Use two points far apart on the line.
fields.problem: The graph shows net force against acceleration for one cart. Find the cart's mass.
fields.q1_b:
Read two points
off the line
fields.q2_b: m = slope = ΔF/Δa

fields.headline:
3.5
Net Force & Acceleration
fields.subhead: Go from a free body diagram to a net force to an acceleration.

imageSubjects.section: an elevator shaft seen from below, cables catching the light

fields.headline: From FBD to Acceleration
fields.subhead: Example: a 10 kg cart is pulled 50 N right and 20 N left.

fields.headline: Pulling at an Angle
fields.subhead: Frictionless ice. Only the horizontal part of the pull speeds it up.
fields.problem: A 20 kg sled is pulled with 60 N at 35° above horizontal. Find a and the normal force.
fields.q2_b:
a = F cos(angle)/m
N = mg − F sin(angle)

fields.headline: Sliding Down a Frictionless Ramp
fields.subhead: Use down the slope as positive.
fields.problem: An 8.0 kg box slides down a frictionless 20° ramp. Find its acceleration.
fields.q2_b:
Fnet = mg sin(angle)
a = g sin(angle)

fields.headline: Elevators and Apparent Weight
fields.subhead: A bathroom scale measures how hard it pushes up on you.
fields.c1_b:
The normal force N,
not your weight.
fields.c2_b:
Fnet = 0, so N = mg.
The scale reads your
true weight.
fields.mustwrite: Accelerating elevator: N − mg = ma, with up as positive.

fields.headline: Elevator Speeding Up, Going Up
fields.subhead: Use up as positive. True weight: 686 N.
fields.problem: A 70 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating up at 2.0 m/s². Find the reading.
fields.q2_b:
N − mg = ma
N = m(g + a)
fields.answer: Scale reads 826 N, more than 686 N

fields.headline: Elevator Accelerating Down
fields.subhead: Use up as positive, so the acceleration is negative.
fields.problem: The same 70 kg person rides an elevator accelerating down at 2.0 m/s². Find the reading.
fields.q2_b:
N − mg = ma
N = m(g − 2.0)
fields.answer: Scale reads 546 N, less than 686 N

fields.headline:
3.6
Frictional Forces
fields.subhead: Find friction from the normal force, and decide whether an object slides.

imageSubjects.section: a heavy wooden crate on a rough concrete floor, scuff marks behind it

fields.headline: Friction
fields.subhead: Friction acts along the surface and opposes sliding.
fields.k1_b:
Along the surface,
against the sliding
(or the would-be sliding).
fields.k2_b:
Holds a resting object.
Matches the push, up to
fs,max = μs N.
fields.k3_b:
Acts while sliding.
fk = μk N, constant.
Usually less than fs,max.
fields.mustwrite: Friction = μN. It depends on the normal force, not directly on the weight.

fields.headline: Constant Velocity
fields.subhead: Constant velocity means Fnet = 0, so friction equals the push.
fields.problem: A 40 kg box is pushed across the floor at constant velocity with 120 N. Find μk.
fields.q1_b:
m = 40 kg
push = 120 N
constant velocity
fields.q2_b:
fk = push
μk = fk/N

fields.headline: Will It Move?
fields.subhead: Compare the push with the maximum static friction first.
fields.problem: A 25 kg box is pushed with 90 N. Does it move? If the push rises to 110 N, find a.
fields.q2_b:
fs,max = μs N
fk = μk N
fields.answer: 90 N: no motion  ·  110 N: a = 1.5 m/s²

fields.headline: Pulling at an Angle with Friction
fields.subhead: The upward part of the pull lowers N, and lowers friction.
fields.problem: A 30 kg crate is pulled with 150 N at 30° above horizontal. μk = 0.25. Find N and a.
fields.q2_b:
N = mg − F sin(angle)
Fnet = F cos(angle) − μk N

fields.headline: Friction on an Incline
fields.subhead: Same tilted axes as 3.3, plus one more force along the slope.
fields.a1_b: Up the slope, against the sliding.
fields.a2_b: N = mg cos(angle), the same as in 3.3.
fields.a3_b: Slides only if mg sin(angle) > μs N.

fields.headline: Does the Block Slide?
fields.subhead: Run the test first. Use down the slope as positive.
fields.problem: A 10 kg block rests on a 35° incline. μs = 0.50, μk = 0.40. Does it slide? If so, find a.
fields.q2_b:
test: mg sin vs μs N
Fnet = mg sin − μk N

fields.headline:
3.7
Multi-Body Systems
fields.subhead: Solve pulley systems as one object for a, then one mass alone for tension.

imageSubjects.section: a steel pulley wheel and rope hanging in a workshop

fields.headline: Ideal Strings and Pulleys
fields.subhead: Massless string, frictionless pulley: the string just changes direction.
fields.c1_b:
One tension T all
along the string.
One size of a for all.
fields.c2_b:
System: a = Fnet/total m.
Then one mass alone
for T.
fields.mustwrite: Solve the whole system for a first, then one mass alone for T.

fields.headline: Atwood Machine
fields.subhead: The heavier mass goes down. Use its direction as positive.
fields.problem: A 5.0 kg mass and a 3.0 kg mass hang over a pulley. Find a and the string tension.

fields.headline: Block on a Table
fields.subhead: Frictionless table. Only the hanging weight drives the system.
fields.problem: A 4.0 kg block on a table is tied over a pulley to a 2.0 kg hanging mass. Find a and T.
fields.q2_b:
a = m2 g/(m1 + m2)
T = m1 a

fields.headline: Block on a Table, with Friction
fields.subhead: Same setup, now μk = 0.20 between block and table.
fields.problem: Repeat the table problem with μk = 0.20. Find a and T.
fields.q2_b:
Fnet = m2 g − μk m1 g
T = m1 a + fk

fields.headline: Challenge: Incline and Pulley
fields.subhead: Frictionless incline. Decide which way it moves first.
fields.problem: A 6.0 kg block on a 30° incline is tied over a pulley to a 5.0 kg hanging mass. Find a and T.
fields.q2_b:
Fnet = m2 g − m1 g sin(angle)
T = m2(g − a)
